strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant NLP problem: combining task adaptation with low-bit quantization. Quantizing the merged base and LoRA weights while learning group-wise scales and offsets is a plausible approach that avoids separate high-precision adapters at inference. Freezing the base weights also reduces optimizer storage relative to full-parameter QAT.

Table 2 provides encouraging results across five LLaMA/LLaMA 2 model variants and both 3-bit and 4-bit settings. L4Q improves every reported commonsense QA average over GPTQ+LoRA, with 3-bit gains of 2.0–3.7 percentage points. The 4-bit results generally remain close to the full-precision LoRA baseline.

The manuscript provides algorithmic pseudocode, many training hyperparameters, and training memory/time measurements. Its ablations address relevant design choices, including quantizer initialization and joint scale/offset learning.
weaknesses: The central memory-saving claim relative to LoRA is not adequately established. L4Q uses BF16 optimizer states while baselines use FP32, without a matched-precision comparison demonstrating why ordinary LoRA cannot obtain similar savings. For Table 4's 10.1M trainable LoRA parameters, halving the precision of two Adam moment tensors saves approximately 0.04 GB, which cannot explain the reported 54.64 versus 25.36 GB difference. A measured breakdown of model, activation, gradient, and optimizer storage is needed. This unresolved attribution is a decisive reason to request revision before recommending Findings.

The backward equations are inconsistent with the stated forward computation. Equations (8)–(9) omit the LoRA scaling factor alpha and leave the treatment of clipping unclear. In Equation (13), the unclipped scale derivative should contain R((w-b_w)/s_w) - (w-b_w)/s_w under the stated rounding STE, but the expression omits b_w despite learning it. These could be presentation errors, but the manuscript must establish which backward procedure produced the results.

Comparative efficiency is difficult to assess because training schedules and configurations differ substantially: L4Q uses 0.2K steps, GPTQ+LoRA 0.4K, and LoRA 1.6K; QA-LoRA additionally uses a different batch size and quantization group size. Table 1's statement about matched training conditions needs reconciliation with these schedules. Matched-budget comparisons or accuracy-versus-compute curves would strengthen the evidence. The closest QA-LoRA comparison is also restricted to LLaMA 7B commonsense QA.

MMLU results support a more qualified performance claim. L4Q has lower reported averages than GPTQ+LoRA in five of six five-shot comparisons. At 4-bit 13B, it scores 41.3 versus 42.1 zero-shot and 44.3 versus 46.9 five-shot. The discussion should acknowledge these trade-offs rather than broadly asserting superior preservation of model quality. No variability estimates establish the reliability of smaller differences.

The ablation specification contains material inconsistencies. Table 4 lists 56.7M trainable parameters for the Min–Max scale-only variant, 113.4M for the AbsMax scale-only variant, and the same 113.4M after adding trainable biases. This conflicts with the described changes and obscures causal interpretation. The initialization parameter gamma is also mentioned without definition in the method. Only upstream library links are supplied, without an L4Q implementation or complete execution and evaluation configurations to resolve these ambiguities.

Deployment benefits remain partly prospective. There are no inference latency measurements or activation-quantization experiments demonstrating the proposed integer-computation advantage. Table 1 shows substantially higher training memory than GPTQ+LoRA, and compressed weight storage during L4Q training is explicitly unimplemented. The 33B single-GPU result is useful but uses a training sequence length of only 128 tokens, limiting its practical generality.
